Issued at 327 PM CDT Sat Sep 5 2026

The Omega-block pattern will remain the focal point of the short- 
term forecast with little changes to overall upper-level flow in the 
last 24 hours or so. Peak heating is expected to resemble that of 
yesterday given a lack of any other potential limiting factors. Just 
before 9 AM Saturday, several sites across the region had already 
started reporting heat index values in the upper 80s and lower 90s. 
Given the fact that several sites were comfortably overachieving 
forecast temperatures by 3-5 degrees this morning, afternoon 
temperatures and highs were nudged up slightly. With temperatures 
climbing into the upper 90s as we progress through the afternoon, we 
could see widespread heat index values of 105F across much of 
Missouri and far eastern Kansas. Some locations may be able to 
surpass this 105F threshold, primarily those in our southernmost 
counties where there's a 60-80% chance of air temperatures hitting 
or exceeding 100F. 

With a backdoor cold front moving through overnight, temperatures 
across northern Missouri are expected to top somewhere in the upper 
80s (NE MO) or low/mid 90s (NW MO). This temperature reduction looks 
to prevent widespread triple digit heat index values, and so the 
Extreme Warning for these portions of the state will come to an end 
around 8 PM today. Unfortunately, not all will be able to reap the 
benefits of this "cold" front tomorrow as recent guidance has this 
boundary coming to a halt generally north and west of the Missouri 
River. As the day progresses, the front should begin to creep to the 
southwest, but it doesn't appear to be early enough to mitigate the 
effects of diurnal heating. Temperatures in the mid/upper 90s are 
currently forecast along and south of the I-70 corridor on Sunday, 
but if the front is able to surge further south earlier in the day, 
it could prevent these maximum temperatures from being realized. 

Another consideration for Sunday is the potential for showers and 
thunderstorms to develop in the afternoon and evening hours. Cooling 
mid-level temperatures and steepening lapse rates ahead of the 
boundary may permit scattered air-mass thunderstorm development in a 
strong warm-air advection regime. Generally speaking, most storms 
should be your run-of-the-mill ordinary thunderstorm, but forecast 
soundings adopt a noteworthy inverted-V shape so downburst winds are 
certainly not out of the question. It's possible we could also see a 
few stronger updrafts conducive of hail production but am not as 
convinced on that threat as of yet. CAMs draw in additional 
convection from the Northern Plains during the evening hours though 
it's unclear how this may evolve in our area with worsening 
instability...current thinking is that any convection that does move 
in from the north will rapidly lose intensity after sunset, though 
strong wind gusts may be possible initially. SPC has highlighted 
much of the CWA in a Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5), encompassing both 
of these possibilities. Overall, there's about a 30-50% chance of 
showers/storms across northern Missouri Sunday evening. Further 
south and east, probabilities are lesser at around 20-30%. 

The backdoor cold front will have completed its journey through the 
CWA by Monday morning. This should result in somewhat cooler 
conditions across the region, especially in central portions of 
Missouri, hence the portion of the Extreme Heat Warning extending 
from St. Joseph to Boonville will end at 8 PM on Sunday. A third 
section of the Extreme Heat Warning that includes the Kansas City 
Metro will be allowed to remain in effect until Tuesday evening at 8 
PM. Conditions on Monday in the vicinity of the Kansas City Metro 
and south appear borderline enough to warrant the continuation of 
the warning for now, especially considering the widespread Major 
(Level 3 of 4) and Extreme (Level 4 of 4) HeatRisk despite slightly 
lesser temperatures and heat index values. Moreover, heat is 
expected to recover on Tuesday, extending the already prolonged heat 
event. Uncertainty still exists in regards to Wednesday as the 
thermal ridge collapses and a low-pressure system marches along the 
northern US border. This system will bring another cold front 
through the region, but the timing of the frontal passage will 
dictate whether heat headlines need to be extended through Wednesday 
or not. As this frontal passage is better resolved in the guidance, 
a decision will be made on whether an extension is necessary. To end 
the week, expect closer to normal temperatures in the mid/upper 80s 
and low 90s in addition to more shower and storm chances as 
shortwaves snake through a more zonal pattern.
